channel.title: iRecord Updates
channel.description: Updates for iRecord - Professional screen recording

item.title: Version 1.264.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.264.0

Changed

  • The editor gives the picture more room — the row of round buttons between the video and the timeline is gone, and what was on it has moved somewhere better. Play now sits on the timeline bar with everything else about time. The scissors sits on the playhead itself, right where the cut will land, and only appears when you are somewhere you can cut. Undo, redo and stepping a frame at a time are keys now — and the timeline tells you which ones, because the app has had these shortcuts all along and never said so anywhere you would see them. Removing a single clip has moved to the right-click menu on the clip, next to everything else you can do to it.
  • The touch-up panel opens on the things you actually change — Camera and Cursor Zoom now sit at the top, and they are the two that are open when the panel is. Crop, Background and Padding start closed. The panel used to open all five at once, which made it taller than the window, so Cursor Zoom sat off the bottom of the screen and you had to scroll down to it every single time. A closed section still says when it is doing something — Cropped, Image, 12% — so nothing you set can hide behind it.
  • A series name stands out from the recordings under it — it was the same size and the same colour as the date on every card below it, so the thing that grouped your recordings read as quieter than a timestamp. It is now larger and brighter, with a small amber marker where each group starts.

Fixed

  • Pointing at a window now gives you the window on top — where two windows overlapped, iRecord chose whichever app's name came first in the alphabet instead of the one under your pointer, so it kept landing on the same app wherever you clicked. It now picks the window you can actually see there.
  • The list of windows keeps up while you arrange them — opening a window, closing one, or bringing a different one to the front all happen while iRecord is in the background, and the New Recording screen was still showing the list from when you opened it. It now looks again each time you come back to iRecord.
  • The crop panel says what it kept, in words — it read 100% × 88% of the source, which has the shape of a video size and left you to work out which number was which, and whether it was what survived or what was cut. It now says Keeping the full width and 88% of the height.

item.title: Version 1.258.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.258.0

Added

  • Group your recordings into a series — recordings that belong together can now be labelled as one. Right-click any recording on Home, or use the ⋯ button on its card or in the editor, and pick Series ▸. Home then shows them together under that name, and searching the series name finds all of them. A series is just a label: nothing moves on your Mac, no files are touched, and picking the same one again takes the recording back out. Renaming a series renames it everywhere at once.
  • Reuse a recording you already set up — mark a recording Use as Template from the same menu, and New Recording gains a From Template list. Starting from one gives you a fresh recording with the same sections, the same script, the same planned lengths and the same look, and none of the old footage. The original is left exactly as it was.
  • Record your whole plan in one go — with sections planned ahead, pressing ● Record next section now records the rest of them in one run: one countdown, and ⌘⇧↓ moves you on to the next section without stopping. The teleprompter follows along, showing each section's script as you reach it, and every section's take lands on the section you planned it against. Stopping partway is fine — the sections you didn't reach are still there, still planned.
  • Plan a recording before you shoot it — you can now write your sections down first. In the editor, press Plan Sections…, paste one line per section, and iRecord turns them into a checklist you record against. Add a length to any line if you want one — Warm-up 2:00, 90s kick drill, Freestyle pull — 1:30 — and a new row above the timeline shows the shape of the whole thing before you have shot a frame: solid blocks for what you have recorded, outlined ones for what is still to come. ● Record next section now records the next section you planned instead of adding one on the end.
  • See how long you are running — where you planned a length, iRecord tells you how the real thing compares: on each section, and at the top of the editor as 8 of 12 sections · 22:40 of 30:00. It counts what you actually kept, so trimming a section that ran long brings it back in line. It only tells you; nothing goes red and nothing stops you saving.
  • Save the same video at several shapes in one go — a video that had to go out square, tall and wide meant three trips through Save. The Save screen now has a Variants list: add the shapes you need, press Save once, and iRecord writes one file per shape into a folder you pick. Each row shows the exact size of the file it will make. Changing a shape here does not change your recording — it stays set up the way you left it.
  • Save the picture on screen as an image — there is a new button next to Save Video that saves the frame you are parked on as a PNG, with your background, your camera and everything else exactly as the video would have it. Move the playhead to the frame you want and press it.
  • Start a section over without stopping the recording — flub a line and your only way out was to stop the whole thing, then set the same shot up again from scratch. There is now a ↺ button next to Pause: it counts you back in with 3-2-1 and starts the section again with everything exactly as you had it. What you recorded up to that point is kept as a take, so you can still go back to it in the editor.
  • See what a recording has produced — every video and poster you save is now listed in the editor, next to Save Video, with when you saved it and whether it still matches what is on the canvas. Trim a clip after saving and the row says Edited since saved, so you know which file is the old one. Home shows the same thing on each card: Recorded, Saved · 3, or Edited since saved.

Fixed

  • Renaming a recording now renames its folder on your Mac, too — renaming only ever changed the name shown inside iRecord, so Finder kept showing Untitled Recording 2, 3, 4 no matter what you called it. The folder now catches up once you leave the editor.
  • Saved videos now start playing straight away when uploaded anywhere — every video iRecord saved was written with its index at the end of the file, so a browser had to download the whole thing before it could show the first frame. The index is now at the front, so a video posted to a website or sent through a link starts as soon as it begins to arrive.
  • Your background image no longer disappears if you move or delete the original — picking an image for the background remembered where it was on your Mac, so moving or deleting that file turned the background black in the editor and in the saved video without a word. iRecord now keeps its own copy inside the recording, copies existing ones in when you open them, and if a copy can't be made the Background panel says so.

Fixed

  • A recording no longer keeps playing after you leave the editor — press play, then go back to Home, and the sound carried on with nothing on screen to pause it. Deleting the recording didn't stop it either; only quitting iRecord did. Leaving the editor now stops playback.

item.title: Version 1.245.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.245.0

Added

  • Put your camera where you want it by dragging it — the New Recording screen used to offer Position and Size as two menus, and you only found out what they meant after recording. The camera is now the control: drag it to a corner of the preview, drag its inner corner to resize, and what you see is what gets saved. Shape is still a choice in the Camera button.
  • The New Recording screen is bigger, and nothing is hidden below a scroll — the preview is now over three times the size it was and fills the top of the window, with every setting as one row of buttons underneath instead of four stacked panels you had to scroll through. How much recording time your free disk space will hold is now at the top, where you can see it before you start rather than once it is nearly gone.
  • The New Recording screen now shows you the recording — the top of it is a live picture of exactly what will be captured, with your camera already in the corner it will end up in. If your screen hasn't changed yet it says so rather than spinning; if the window you picked has closed, or another app has taken your camera, it tells you there and then instead of after the countdown. Picking a window now works like the Mac's own screenshot tool: click Choose window…, the screen dims, and you point at the window you want. With two displays you click the one you mean, laid out the way they really sit on your desk.
  • The countdown happens over that picture — the preview freezes on its last frame and 3-2-1 counts over it, so you can see what you are about to record right up to the moment it starts.

Fixed

  • The New Recording preview no longer has black bars down the sides — the picture of your screen was being fitted into a box that was the wrong shape for most Macs, so there was a black strip on the left and right of everything you previewed. The box is now the shape of whatever you are recording, so the picture fills it. The row of buttons underneath has more room around it and sits centred.
  • The camera in the New Recording preview now moves as you do — it only redrew when something on your screen changed, so while you were talking to a still window your own face sat there as a frozen photograph that jumped every few seconds. The camera now updates on its own, whatever the screen is doing.
  • The New Recording screen no longer feels sluggish while the preview is running — every new frame of the preview was redrawing the whole screen around it, so the faster the camera got the heavier everything else became. The picture now updates on its own without touching the rest of the window.
  • The New Recording preview is sharp — it was being drawn at half the detail your display can show, which made the whole picture, and your camera in particular, look soft and small. It now draws at full resolution.
  • iRecord could quit unexpectedly while you were setting up a recording — two problems on the New Recording screen, both fixed: the dimming overlay used for picking a window was cleaned up in a way that could leave the app pointing at something no longer there, and the screen was asking your Mac which camera to use twelve times a second while you had it open.
  • The editor showed your camera slightly further from the edge than the saved file put it — the preview and the export worked out the camera's margin two different ways, so they agreed only at one particular window width and drifted either side of it. They now use the same one. Your saved videos are unchanged; it is the preview that was off.
  • Where you put the camera on the New Recording screen is where it appears in your video — Position, Size and Shape only ever changed the little camera bubble floating on your screen while you recorded. The saved video ignored all three, so choosing Top Left still put the camera in the bottom right corner, a Rectangle came out a circle, and the camera was a little bigger in the video than the bubble had been. All three now carry through to what you save.
  • Camera size is a percentage on both screens — the New Recording screen offered Small, Medium and Large while the editor offered a percentage, and they did not mean the same thing. Both now say the same number, and if you had picked one of the three words it keeps the size the bubble showed you while you recorded. One side effect worth knowing: because the saved video used to ignore this setting completely, your next recording's camera may come out a little smaller than your last one's. Set whatever size you like on either screen.

item.title: Version 1.243.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.243.0

Fixed

  • Recording a window no longer leaves a black strip down one side of the video — for some windows, iRecord asked for a slightly wrong size before recording started, so the picture didn't quite fill the frame it was given and the leftover space showed up black in every frame. iRecord now checks the real size right before it starts and uses that instead. Full-screen recordings were never affected.
  • Deleting a Recording now really deletes it — the Recording disappeared from iRecord as it should, but an empty folder was left behind on your Mac every single time. They piled up quietly where your recordings are kept, and nothing ever cleared them. Nothing is left behind now.
  • A quiet hiccup could throw away your edits — when iRecord couldn't write one small companion file next to a take, it gave up on saving that Recording altogether, so the trims and splits you had just made were lost without a word. The companion file is now skipped if it can't be written, and your edits are saved either way.
  • Cropping your recording now fills the frame instead of leaving black bars — the trimmed picture used to play back inside the shape it had before you cropped it, so it looked smaller than the area you drew, with dark gaps where the trimmed edges used to be. The video now reshapes to exactly what you crop, in the editor and in the saved file.

item.title: Version 1.241.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.241.0

Added

  • Crop your screen recording right in the editor — say your window recording caught a row of browser tabs you'd rather not show. Open Edit and Crop is right there at the top; draw the area you want to keep and the rest is trimmed away in both the editor and your saved video.
  • A trash icon in the editor deletes a Recording without hunting for a right-click menu — that was the only way to delete a Recording from inside the editor before. Save Video and Edit also lost their text labels in favour of a tidier row of icons next to it (hover any of them for a reminder of what it does). Deleting still asks you to confirm first, since it can't be undone.
  • The timeline blocks show the sound in your recording — finding the pause where you stopped to think meant scrubbing back and forth watching the picture, because every block was a flat colour. Each block now draws the shape of its own sound, and a silence reads as a flat line along the bottom. Nothing about the recording changes; it is only easier to see where to cut.
  • The New Recording window says what is about to spoil the take — a cluttered desktop, a chat app that is one message away from showing on screen, a battery about to run out. These are easy to miss until you watch the recording back, so iRecord now lists them before you press Record. It only looks: nothing on your Mac is changed or switched off, and you can start recording whatever it says.
  • Re-record one part of a section without redoing the rest — if you had cut a section in two and wanted to redo only the second half, re-recording replaced both halves with the new take, so the first half stopped playing what you had recorded for it. Right-clicking a block now offers Re-record this Part alongside Re-record the Whole Section. The part you pick is the only one that changes, and every other block plays exactly what it played before.

Fixed

  • Your face and your voice are back in sync — the camera video started counting from the moment the camera woke up rather than from the moment the recording began, so everything it filmed played about a second early and your lips ran ahead of what you were saying. The camera now starts where the recording starts. If the camera takes a moment to wake up, that moment is simply blank instead of shifting the whole thing.
  • Choosing a window no longer offers you pieces of a window — some apps quietly keep extra windows open for their own toolbars and menus. These were listed alongside real windows, with nothing but the app's name on them, so two Chrome entries looked identical and picking the wrong one recorded a thin black strip instead of the page. Only real windows are offered now, and when two of them share a name the list shows their size so you can tell which is which.
  • The shortcut for stopping a recording actually stops it — the menu said ⌘⇧. stops recording, but it only worked while iRecord itself was in front, which is never the case while you are recording something else. It now works from any app, for as long as a recording is running.
  • Stopping from the floating bar takes one click, not two — clicking Stop while another app was in front spent the first click bringing iRecord forward, which on a full-screen recording put iRecord's own window into the video. The first click now stops the recording and iRecord stays out of the way.
  • The floating recording bar stays where you put it — dragging it out of the way worked until the next recording, when it went back to the top of the screen. It now reappears where you left it, including after you unplug an external display.
  • The file size shown before you save is now a limit, not a guess — the number on the Save screen was the most the video could weigh, but it was written as though it were the size you would get. Saved files often came in a lot smaller, because a recording of a mostly still screen compresses much further than a busy one. It now reads up to 31 MB, and the file you get is never bigger than that.
  • Re-recording a section could hide part of the take you just made — if you had split a section and then re-recorded it, only as much of the new take as the old one was long stayed on the timeline. Anything past that point was saved to disk but left out of your video, with nothing on screen to say so. The whole take now appears, and a note tells you it came out longer. If you had deliberately trimmed the end off a section, that trim is still respected.
